articles.title: OpenAI valued at $1.25 trillion, as rival Anthropic nears its IPO

articles.full_text:
AI Business News OpenAI valued at $1.25 trillion, as rival Anthropic nears its IPO CEO Sam Altman said recently that OpenAI is prioritizing safety instead of going ‘guns blazing’ toward an IPO.﻿ CEO Sam Altman said recently that OpenAI is prioritizing safety instead of going ‘guns blazing’ toward an IPO.﻿ by Stevie Bonifield Nov 6, 2026, 11:46 PM UTC Link Share Gift Image: The Verge Stevie Bonifield is a news writer covering all things consumer tech.

Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

OpenAI is now valued at $1.25 trillion in a new round of funding that has raised another $11 billion, according to Bloomberg .

That would make it one of the world’s most valuable companies, not long after raising $122 billion from investors in March at a valuation of $852 billion.

Echoing FT and Wall Street Journal reports from last week, Bloomberg says OpenAI is still pursuing additional investments that could increase the amount to $20 billion, and that it had initially hoped to raise as much as $30 billion at a higher valuation of $1.4 trillion.

That was before tech stocks dropped, and the results of the midterms showed how much public opinion has turned against AI companies and data center projects .

OpenAI’s rival Anthropic filed its S-1 to go public last week.

Earlier this year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said it’s holding off on its own IPO until it can make more confident claims about its models’ safety.

He didn’t give a specific timeline for the IPO, but said at the time, “I think it’s also kind of bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

articles.title: OpenAI reportedly raises an additional $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI product & news、Startup & business
articles.summary: OpenAI has reportedly raised an additional $11 billion as part of a funding round that hasn't closed yet but is expected to in the coming weeks.
articles.full_text:
In Brief Posted: 2:53 PM PST · November 6, 2026 Lucas Ropek OpenAI reportedly raises an additional $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation OpenAI has reportedly raised $11 billion so far in a new funding round that values the AI lab at $1.25 trillion.

Bloomberg reported on the new funding on Friday, citing sources familiar with the matter.

The $11 billion is part of a larger funding round that hasn’t closed yet, according to the outlet.

The round is expected to close in the coming weeks and could total about $20 billion, a source told Bloomberg.

In late September, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI was looking to raise $30 billion in the upcoming round.

The current figures fall well short of that target.

TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment and will update this story if it responds.

The news comes only hours after Bloomberg also reported that potential buyers of shares in the IPO of OpenAI’s chief competitor, Anthropic, are eyeing a substantially lower valuation than Anthropic had targeted.

Bloomberg writes that some potential buyers believe Anthropic’s valuation could be as low as $1.1 trillion, compared with the $2 trillion that investors were said to be expecting roughly a month ago.

OpenAI previously intimated that it would go public this year but subsequently delayed its plans.

There are expectations that the company will IPO next year at some point.

The market for AI hangs in a particularly precarious place.

The Democratic landslide in the U.S. midterms — and overwhelmingly negative voter sentiment around data centers — has caused jitters throughout the market , with many anticipating potential regulatory challenges in the future.

articles.title: Ramp data shows AI spending stalling just as Anthropic nears its IPO
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI product & news、Startup & business
articles.summary: AI usage keeps climbing, but spending has stalled. Price cuts and smarter cost controls among the biggest spenders could challenge investor assumptions about AI hypergrowth.
articles.full_text:
Companies are using more AI than ever, but they’re not spending more on it.

A new report from Ramp shows AI spending flatlined over late summer even as token volumes rose, a sign that price competition and savvier customers may be capping revenue for OpenAI and Anthropic.

According to Ramp’s data, token spend only grew 1.5% across August and September.

To compare, in July, it grew 42% from the previous month.

As Anthropic gears up for its IPO , the data suggests investors might be wrong to assume AI companies will keep growing at breakneck speed. “Almost the entire spend on AI is from venture-backed, high-growth tech companies,” Ramp’s lead economist Ara Kharazian told TechCrunch. “That’s fine as long as AI spend continues to rise, but if it starts to slow down because of something in the market or some other factor, they will all start to slow down simultaneously, and that could lead to other cascading effects.” Kharazian said he’s already seeing evidence that the top 1% of firms — the most “ AI-pilled ” — have stuttered slightly in their spend in August and September, coming up just below the $10,000 per-employee they were hitting at their summer peaks.

A slowdown among that cohort is “sufficient to slow down revenue entirely, despite the fact that we’re seeing rising volumes,” he said.  Ramp data shows growth in spending among median and top 10%, but it’s not enough to make up the difference.

Median firms spend $12-$15 per employee per month, and the top 10% spend $600-$1,000.  “If you look at the use cases today, it’s not necessarily clear they will get up to that $10,000 per employee per month mark that the 1% is at,” Kharazian said.

While there’s plenty of demand for AI coding agents in industries like software and finance, “it’s not necessarily true that a doctor’s office or a car dealership will need to spend that much on AI.” “The era of hypergrowth may be over, and now that we know there may not be as much juice to squeeze out of the top 1%,” he continued.

October data did see a re-acceleration, with token spend up 8.9% from September 23 to October 23, but Kharazian said the headwinds on spend growth are strong.

Kharazian (who has published a series of blogs called “ Cracks in the AI Thesis ”) said the slowdown isn’t due to a demand problem.

Again, AI volumes are up.

Instead he points to the competitive nature of the marketplace. “OpenAI and Anthropic price cuts have…just made it cheaper to use AI,” he said.

In September, OpenAI cut API prices in half for GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna.

Answering the price war, Anthropic has also made significant reductions to pricing for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 — a decision that the company said in a recent filing slashed revenue growth by about $600 million.

Both companies have also been offering enterprise discounts that are intended to lock-in spend, but in reality are hitting their revenue targets.

Kharazian said this dynamic means it has very much become a buyer’s market.

Subsidizing use of expensive technology in order to lock in customers has always been a part of the Big Tech playbook.

Just recall how cheap it used to be to take an Uber or Lyft ride, and now that there are few other ride-hail players, the cost of going from A to B has risen significantly.

Kharazian says those dynamics don’t work in the AI world because there’s just too much competition. “Meta and Nvidia are also introducing enterprise offerings with pretty cheap models or open source models,” Kharazian said.

He also pointed to the range of other open model companies from China and the United States, as well as a new company called Jev — a lightweight tool for choosing between a few predetermined outputs — that is increasingly among the top performers on Ramp. “For a lot of AI use cases, you just need a simple Yes/No,” Kharazian said. “So you take your already cheap models, you shift them over to Jev, and now your already cheap stuff gets even cheaper.” The ability to complete workloads at a much cheaper cost is another factor driving the spending slowdown.

That’s partly due to the discounts from AI companies, but also because companies are just getting better at being thrifty. “As you get really advanced in using AI, you get better at figuring out how to control it,” Kharazian said. “You’re more likely to use defaults that prevent usage of very expensive models for long-running tasks.

You’re more likely to impose some budgets on employees.

You’re more likely to offload some of the spend from standard and light models to even cheaper light models via routers.” Notion co-founder Akshay Kothari recently posted internal data that matched Ramp’s insights.

As he succinctly put it: “tokens go brrr. costs go ahhh.” “A lot of the assumptions that we had about the trajectory of AI spend are starting to break down,” Kharazian said. “You can use more AI, but use it for less.

That’s great for the customers…but it’s not necessarily great for the model companies.

And it does introduce new questions around their revenue trajectories.” Bloomberg reported Friday that Anthropic’s potential valuation sank from the $2 trillion estimated in early October to just $1.2 to $1.3 trillion.

The company is also reportedly expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit agencies.

OpenAI also lowered its proposed valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion and slashed its latest fundraising goals by about $10 billion.  Kharazian says Ramp’s dataset likely informs many investor concerns.

There is, however, one potential brightside for spending trajectories, albeit a speculative one.

Much of the thesis for hypergrowth spending is that AI will undoubtedly introduce new use cases that will accelerate things.

AI coding emerged just a year and a half ago as the most commercially viable product that has led Anthropic and OpenAI to becoming trillion-dollar companies.

The hope among investors is that there will be another revolution that will drive further spend.  Some think personal agents will be the next coding agents.

OpenAI , SpaceXAI , and Meta have all released their own personal agents, alongside startups like Instinct .

Kharazian is skeptical, though, that personal agents, which are “not as economically productive as coding,” will provide the boost the industry needs for nonstop growth. “The projection is that there will be new products being introduced that will drive further growth,” Kharazian said. “But based on what we can observe today and the products available and what is commercially advanced, AI spend has started to slow down.” Topics AI , Anthropic , Enterprise , Enterprise AI spend , OpenAI , Ramp When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission .

articles.title: Palo Alto Networks in talks to buy AI agent security startup Clutch for $500M
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI agent & application、Startup & business
articles.summary: Clutch, backed by Lightspeed and SignalFire, was last valued at $85 million, according to a source.
articles.full_text:
Palo Alto Networks is in talks to acquire Clutch Security , a startup that secures AI agents’ access to company systems, for $500 million in cash plus additional milestone-based payouts, according to a person familiar with the discussions.

Three-year-old Clutch was last valued at $85 million when it raised a $20 million Series A round in January 2025, led by Lightspeed and SignalFire, according to our source.

The startup is currently approaching $10 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR).

That means the acquisition, if completed, would value Clutch at about 50 times its ARR, a standard way of pricing software companies.

Palo Alto Networks and Clutch Security did not respond to a request for comment.

The Information was the first to report the acquisition discussions.

The high valuation is not an anomaly in a market increasingly focused on securing software against bad actors using AI to breach systems more easily.

Upwind, a startup using AI to secure cloud infrastructure, recently turned down an acquisition offer from Datadog that valued it at roughly 40 times ARR, TechCrunch reported last week.

If the deal happens, it would be Palo Alto Networks’ seventh acquisition this year, according to PitchBook.

The cybersecurity giant has a history of buying innovation rather than building it in-house, and it has ramped up dealmaking this year in response to rising AI-driven cyberattacks.

In September, Palo Alto Networks acquired Console, a two-year-old startup that uses AI agents to automate routine IT help desk tasks.

The transaction valued Console at $500 million in stock and cash, TechCrunch reported.

Other VC-backed companies that Palo Alto Networks has scooped up this year include NEA-backed Embrace, for $325 million ; Chronosphere, an observability platform backed by Greylock and Lux Capital, for $2.95 billion ; and Koi, a cyber startup backed by Battery and Team8, for $231 million , according to regulatory filings.

Several of Clutch’s competitors have also been acquired.

Cyera, a cybersecurity startup valued at $12 billion earlier this year, acquired Oasis Security, which, like Clutch, focuses on managing AI agents’ access to systems, for $1 billion .

Meanwhile, Cisco bought Menlo Ventures-backed Astrix for roughly $400 million , Calcalist reported.

articles.title: Meta’s Muse AI can create custom ‘spaces’ for the version of the app you need right now
articles.summary: Meta will now allow you to build customized, app-like experiences within Muse. The new feature, called "spaces," allows its AI assistant to build things like a shopping hub, school dashboard, music tracker, trivia game, and more, which you can interact with directly in the Muse app. Meta says you can create a new space by […]
articles.full_text:
Tech AI Apps Meta’s Muse AI can create custom ‘spaces’ for the version of the app you need right now You can create things like a shopping hub, school dashboard, or music tracker directly within Muse.

You can create things like a shopping hub, school dashboard, or music tracker directly within Muse. by Emma Roth Nov 6, 2026, 6:10 PM UTC Link Share Gift Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more.

Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Meta will now allow you to build customized, app-like experiences within Muse.

The new feature, called “spaces,” allows its AI assistant to build things like a shopping hub, school dashboard, music tracker, trivia game, and more, which you can interact with directly in the Muse app.

Meta says you can create a new space by describing it.

If you connect an outside app to Muse — like Gmail, Google Calendar, OpenTable, Notion, and others Muse works with — the AI assistant will continuously pull information from them, allowing it to update pricing, dates, and other information in your space in the background.

You can also interact with elements inside your spaces by checking things off, adding notes, and making edits.

Related Muse has a voice mode now You can also change the placement of your spaces in the Muse app, too, as Meta lets you keep them in the sidebar, move them into your main tab, or schedule when you see them. “For example, keep your weekly planner up front during the workweek, then swap it for your weekend plans on Saturday,” Meta says.

Meta also announced that it’s bringing new “Active Memory” and “Active Focus” capabilities from its Muse Wonder AI model into the Muse app and its Meta AI chatbot.

This will allow Muse to understand when past information becomes relevant during conversations, as well as make it better at working toward goals.

Meta is rolling out spaces to all Muse users.

The company is also looking into ways to share your spaces with other users and collaborate with them.
